advisor.summary: A more-than-2% S corporation shareholder is treated as a partner for fringe-benefit purposes under §1372, so corporate-paid health premiums are not an excludable fringe — they belong in the shareholder's W-2 Box 1. That inclusion is the price of admission, and it is cheap: Announcement 92-16 keeps the amount out of the FICA boxes, and once the premiums have run through wages the shareholder deducts them above the line under §162(l) per the Rev. Rul. 91-26 and Notice 2008-1 framework. The entity deduction and the wage inclusion wash, leaving the §162(l) deduction as the net federal effect — premiums the owner was paying after-tax become an above-the-line deduction at zero payroll-tax cost, which is exactly the transform the model applies. The mechanics forgive nothing: premiums paid personally all year with no entity payment or reimbursement and no W-2 inclusion simply lose the deduction for that year, and mere eligibility for a subsidized employer plan on either spouse's side disallows month by month.
mechanics: §1372 treats the more-than-2% shareholder — and family attributed through the stock-ownership rules, a working spouse included — as a partner for fringe purposes, so the premium is compensation rather than an excludable benefit.

The corporation pays or reimburses the premiums under a documented arrangement, deducts them as compensation, and adds them to W-2 Box 1 only — Boxes 3 and 5 stay untouched because Announcement 92-16 exempts the inclusion from FICA.

With the premiums in wages, the shareholder deducts them above the line under §162(l); Notice 2008-1 confirms the deduction survives even when the policy is in the shareholder's own name, provided the entity paid or reimbursed and the W-2 shows it.

The deduction is capped at the shareholder's W-2 wages from the corporation under §162(l)'s earned-income limit — wages below the premium level shrink the deduction, which ties this strategy to reasonable-compensation planning, and the model caps at wages accordingly.
No deduction is allowed for any calendar month either spouse is merely eligible for a subsidized employer plan (§162(l)(2)(B)) — eligibility, not enrollment, is the test.

authority.note: Partner treatment for more-than-2% shareholders on fringe benefits — the reason the premiums must flow through the W-2.
The above-the-line self-employed health insurance deduction — limited to W-2 wages from the corporation for a 2% shareholder, and disallowed for any month of subsidized-plan eligibility.
Premiums paid for a partner or 2% shareholder-employee are compensation includible in income — the framework's foundation.
The controlling mechanics — entity payment or reimbursement plus W-2 inclusion, or no deduction; policies in the shareholder's own name can qualify.
The Box 1 inclusion is not FICA wages — the rule that makes the routing costless on the payroll side.

requirements: An S corporation paying the shareholder W-2 wages at least equal to the premiums.
Premiums paid by the corporation or reimbursed under a documented arrangement — never left as personal payments with no entity involvement.
Payroll coding that adds the premiums to Box 1 only, with the FICA boxes untouched.
No month of subsidized employer-plan eligibility for either spouse.
risks: The leading failure is procedural and uncurable after year-end: premiums paid personally with no entity payment or reimbursement and no W-2 inclusion forfeit the §162(l) deduction for the year — Notice 2008-1 is explicit, and the exam adjustment writes itself.
A spouse taking a job with subsidized coverage disallows the deduction month by month on eligibility alone, even if the family never enrolls.
W-2 wages below the premium level cap the deduction — coordinate with reasonable-compensation planning before assuming the full amount.
Payroll providers sometimes route the inclusion through the FICA boxes, converting a free adjustment into needless payroll tax — check the coding the first January.
IRS guidance treats the §162(l) deduction as also reducing the shareholder's QBI; the modeled savings do not compute that §199A offset, so flag it where QBI is material.
stateNotes: Missouri conforms: the §162(l) deduction reduces federal AGI, which is the Missouri starting point (RSMo §143.121), so the benefit flows through automatically.

PTET interaction: the premium is an entity-level compensation deduction that shrinks the income base a Missouri pass-through entity tax election is computed on (RSMo §143.436); the engine sequences PTET after this deduction, so no additional state benefit should be layered on.

Missouri-specific: Missouri's own qualified health premium deduction (RSMo §143.113) reaches only premiums not already deducted federally — once this routing is in place there is no second Missouri deduction for the same dollars.
reviewChecklist: Entity payment or documented reimbursement of premiums verified for every month of the year.
W-2 shows the premiums in Box 1 only, with FICA boxes clean — checked against the payroll provider's coding.
Owner W-2 wages meet or exceed premiums, or the modeled deduction reflects the wage cap.
Both spouses' subsidized-coverage eligibility confirmed month by month, with known job changes calendared.
QBI materiality assessed and the unmodeled §199A offset flagged in the plan where relevant.

client.teaser: Turn a bill you already pay every month into a full tax deduction.
client.headline: Deduct your health insurance — the right way for S-corp owners
plainEnglish: If you own an S corporation and pay for your own health insurance, you may be paying with after-tax money — no deduction. The law gives S-corp owners a full deduction, but only if the paperwork flows one specific way.

The company pays the premiums, or pays you back. The amount shows up in your W-2. Then you deduct the whole thing on your personal return. The pieces cancel out except one: a full deduction, with no Social Security or Medicare tax on any of it.
The catch is timing. If the year ends and the premiums never ran through the company and your W-2, the deduction is gone for that year. So the setup happens now, not at tax time.
client.analogy: It is the same money taking a smarter route — like finding out the toll road you drive daily has a free lane, but you must merge into it before your exit.
benefits: Your full health premium becomes a tax deduction
No payroll tax on any of it
No new spending — money you already pay, rerouted
Repeats automatically every year once set up
steps: WE move the premium payments to the company or set up a reimbursement plan.
WE set payroll to report the premiums correctly on your W-2.
WE take the full deduction on your personal return.
YOU tell us right away if either spouse is offered health coverage at another job.
clientCommitments: Keep premium payments running through the company, not your personal account
Tell us about any job change that comes with a health plan offer — even one you decline

Update the reimbursement arrangement and premium amounts at each renewal
